strengths: EA-KD is simple, interpretable, and practically useful: its teacher-student entropy weight can augment both logit- and feature-based distillation without architectural changes and with little apparent overhead.

The empirical scope is strong. On CIFAR-100, EA variants improve 46 of 49 method/architecture combinations, averaging +0.56 points; additional gains appear on Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, transformer-to-CNN distillation, MS-COCO detection, and LLM distillation.

The paper includes useful component and temperature ablations, inverted-weight controls, entropy-stratified analyses, loss-landscape and hyperparameter studies, multiple-run reporting, and publicly identified code. The manuscript is generally clear and positions the method against relevant adaptive and entropy-based KD work. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-v_ozrrdl/call-c8bf2bbdda6f400fb7629b9ed145529d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The favorable results across many existing KD frameworks make this an impactful plug-in contribution despite its incremental conceptual novelty.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is confounded by loss scaling. Since the unnormalized weight lies in [0, log C], EA-KD changes not only the relative importance of samples but also the average magnitude of the distillation loss versus the supervised loss. The specially reduced MLD+LS coefficient compounds this concern. Mean-normalized weighting and an equally scaled uniform-loss control are needed.

The theoretical argument only considers a uniformly initialized student and extreme teacher distributions; it does not establish a general KL-divergence bias or prove that high-entropy examples are valuable. The analogous claim for feature-MSE distillation is asserted without analysis. High entropy can also indicate label noise, ambiguity, teacher error, or miscalibration, none of which is tested.

The incremental benefit of student-adaptive weighting over teacher-only entropy is modest and inconsistent. In Table 9, w_EA trails w_base for FCFD, while Table 2 reports 77.50 for EA-FCFD although Table 9 assigns that value to w_base and reports 77.44 for w_EA. Comparisons with the closest sample-reweighting methods are also limited.

Statistical support is incomplete: supplementary statistics cover the proposed variants but generally not matched baseline reruns, and the authors state that baseline means often come from prior papers. Consequently, several 0.1-0.4 point gains cannot be judged using paired uncertainty estimates; some configurations also regress despite claims of consistency.

Reproducibility from the paper alone is limited for object detection and LLM experiments: the definition and aggregation of entropy, precise loss composition, sample unit, and coefficient normalization are underspecified. The unexplained switch from T'=3 to T'=2 and the absence of timing protocol details also weaken the plug-and-play and negligible-cost claims.

strengths: EA-KD is simple, inexpensive, and potentially easy to integrate into existing logit- and feature-distillation pipelines.
The evaluation is unusually broad: seven teacher–student pairs and seven KD frameworks on CIFAR-100, plus Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, transformer teachers, COCO detection, and an exploratory LLM study.
Most reported comparisons improve over their corresponding baselines, with particularly meaningful gains for vanilla KD on Tiny-ImageNet and for COCO detection.
The paper includes component and temperature ablations, runtime measurements, multiple-run results for several settings, and qualitative analyses intended to explain the behavior.

The manuscript is readable, generally attributes datasets and prior methods appropriately, and provides a code URL :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/iccv2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-5hpnqsjp/call-0b208968694d4874b8ea8f28dd7d17ab/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The main evidence is confounded by loss scale. The entropy weights are not reported as mean-normalized, so EA-KD changes both relative sample importance and the overall distillation-to-supervision coefficient. The authors even reduce MLD+LS's KD weight from 9 to 4 for its EA variant. Constant-weight, tuned-coefficient, and mean-normalized controls are essential to establish that entropy-based prioritization—not simple rescaling—causes the gains.

The theoretical motivation is overclaimed. Equations 5–7 consider only an initially uniform student and extreme teacher distributions; they do not establish a general KL bias toward low-entropy samples. Predictive entropy measures uncertainty, not necessarily useful information, and the asserted connection between feature magnitude and low entropy is unsupported.

Originality is limited relative to RW-KD, PAD, AKD, and especially WTTM's teacher-uncertainty weighting. The teacher–student interaction is heuristic, and its incremental value is weak: it only scales teacher entropy between one-half and one, gives modest gains over teacher-only weighting, and is worse than teacher-only weighting for FCFD in Table 9.

Statistical support is inadequate for many small gains. Standard deviations are reported only for EA variants rather than matched reruns of their baselines; numerous improvements are 0.1–0.4 points, comparable to reported run variation. ImageNet uses one model pair, while detection results lack uncertainty estimates and strong task-specific KD comparisons.

Important implementation details are missing: the complete supervised-plus-distillation objective, batch normalization of weights, whether gradients propagate through student entropy, and precisely how image/proposal/token entropies and losses are aggregated for detection and LLMs. The unexplained use of T'=2 for some settings further weakens reproducibility.

The method may emphasize ambiguous, mislabeled, out-of-distribution, or teacher-misclassified examples. There is no robustness, calibration, label-noise, or teacher-quality analysis, despite the central identification of high uncertainty with high learning value.

Several explanatory results are weak evidence: shifting loss mass after explicitly reweighting it is largely tautological; t-SNE proximity does not establish informativeness; and the underspecified 2D loss-surface/Area@1.6 comparisons do not substantiate generalization. Minor table inconsistencies, including the FCFD ablation value and supplementary citation numbering, also need correction.

strengths: EA-KD is a simple, inexpensive sample-reweighting mechanism that combines teacher and student predictive entropy and can be integrated without architectural changes.

The empirical scope is broad: seven teacher-student pairs and multiple logit/feature distillers on CIFAR-100, plus Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, transformer teachers, COCO detection, and LLM distillation. Most comparisons improve, including +3.39 points over KD on Tiny-ImageNet and +0.76 on ImageNet.
The paper includes component and temperature ablations, multi-run statistics for the proposed variants, loss-distribution analyses, and a comparison with the closely related TTM/WTTM approach.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, and it provides a public code link.
weaknesses: The main results have a serious loss-scale confound. Equation 14 multiplies each distillation loss by an unnormalized weight in [0, log(C)]; with softened predictions these weights can substantially exceed one, thereby changing the overall KD coefficient rather than merely redistributing attention among samples. The special reduction of MLD+LS's KD weight from 9 to 4 reinforces this concern. A mean-one normalization and matched constant-, random-, or permuted-weight controls are essential; the inverted-entropy experiment does not control for scale.

The theoretical motivation is not convincing. Equations 5-7 assume a uniform student and extreme teacher distributions; the high-entropy case has teacher and student distributions equal and therefore correctly produces zero KL, which does not establish an inherent bias against valuable knowledge. Predictive entropy can also represent ambiguity, label noise, miscalibration, or teacher error rather than value. The unsupported feature-magnitude claim and t-SNE-based assertions about decision boundaries do not repair this gap.

Important implementation details are missing: whether gradients through student entropy are detached, how the weighted KD loss is combined with supervised loss, and how classification entropy is defined or aggregated over proposals and tokens for detection and LLM experiments. These choices materially change the objective and limit reproducibility.

The statistical comparison is inadequate for many small gains. The supplement reports deviations only for EA variants because baseline values come from prior papers, rather than rerunning matched baselines with identical seeds. Several gains are only 0.1-0.4 points, some CIFAR-100 results decrease, and the improvements over WTTM overlap reported variation. The stated five-run protocol also conflicts with three-run table captions.

Novelty over prior uncertainty/sample-reweighting methods is incremental, and evidence for the specifically proposed student-dependent interaction is weak: in Table 9, teacher-only weighting is already competitive and even exceeds the full weight for FCFD. The closest-method comparison is limited to three CIFAR-100 pairs, while the broad state-of-the-art claim is based on a selective baseline set. Robustness to noisy, ambiguous, or miscalibrated teachers—a central failure mode of high-entropy emphasis—is not evaluated.

strengths: EA-KD is simple, interpretable, inexpensive, and readily applicable to per-sample distillation losses. Combining fixed teacher entropy with evolving student entropy is practically appealing.

The evaluation is unusually broad: seven teacher-student pairs and seven logit- or feature-based methods on CIFAR-100, plus Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, transformer-to-CNN transfer, MS-COCO detection, and LLM distillation. Improvements are mostly consistent and sometimes substantial, especially for vanilla KD.

The manuscript includes useful supporting analyses: entropy-stratified accuracy, inverted-weight controls, component and temperature ablations, loss allocation across entropy quartiles, loss landscapes, and DKD hyperparameter sensitivity.

The presentation is generally clear, relevant prior work—including PAD, AKD, and WTTM—is discussed, repeated-run statistics are provided for the proposed variants, and a code repository is identified.
weaknesses: The principal experimental confound is that the weights are not normalized: wEA lies in [0, log C], so EA-KD changes the average magnitude of the distillation term and its balance against supervised or auxiliary losses. The paper even reduces the MLD+LS KD coefficient from 9 to 4. Without a unit-mean normalization or a constant-weight baseline matched to the mean wEA, the gains cannot be confidently attributed to sample prioritization rather than ordinary loss-coefficient tuning.

The theoretical argument does not establish the claimed general KLD bias. Equations 5–7 consider only a uniform student and the two extreme teacher distributions; the maximally entropic teacher used in the argument is itself uniform, supplies no class-discriminative knowledge, and yields zero KD gradient. More generally, high predictive entropy denotes uncertainty, not necessarily valuable information, and can arise from teacher errors, ambiguous inputs, label noise, or poor calibration.

Evidence that the student-entropy term is essential is weak. In Table 9, wEA improves over teacher-only wbase by only 0.08–0.32 points for three methods and is worse for FCFD (77.44 versus 77.50), contradicting the table caption; this also conflicts with the 77.50 EA-FCFD result in Table 2. Improvements over the closely related WTTM in Table A1 are likewise very small relative to reported variability.

Statistical comparisons are not well controlled. Standard deviations are reported only for EA variants, while most baselines are literature point estimates rather than paired reruns using identical seeds. Many claimed gains are 0.1–0.5 points and therefore cannot be distinguished from run-to-run variation; COCO and LLM tables also omit uncertainty. The statement that statistical testing is inapplicable does not substitute for rerunning the baselines.

Important implementation details are underspecified: whether gradients flow through the student-entropy weight, the complete objective including hard-label and auxiliary losses, and the precise aggregation used for detection proposals or token-level LLM outputs. The unexplained switch from T'=3 to T'=2 for ImageNet and transformer teachers also weakens the claim of tuning-free deployment.

The broad claim that high-entropy samples carry critical knowledge lacks failure-case evaluation. Figure 2 shows teacher accuracy falling sharply in the highest-entropy group, yet the method does not distinguish informative boundary cases from teacher mistakes. Experiments with noisy labels, miscalibrated or weak teachers, distribution shift, and teacher-correct versus teacher-incorrect subsets are needed to delimit when entropy upweighting is reliable.

strengths: EA-KD is exceptionally simple and inexpensive: the sample-wise weight in Eq. (11) can, in principle, augment both logit- and feature-based distillation without architectural changes.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering seven teacher-student pairs and multiple KD frameworks on CIFAR-100, larger-scale classification, transformer-to-CNN transfer, COCO detection, and GPT-2 distillation. Most reported changes are positive, including substantial gains for vanilla KD on Tiny-ImageNet and COCO.

The paper includes component and temperature ablations, analyses over entropy groups and training epochs, multiple-run results for the proposed variants, computational-cost measurements, and a public code link.
The presentation is generally clear, with explicit equations and useful comparisons to adaptive distillation approaches such as CTKD, PAD, RW-KD, and WTTM.
weaknesses: The central justification is not technically convincing. Equations (5)-(7) compare a uniform student with a low-entropy teacher versus a uniform high-entropy teacher; in the latter case, zero KLD reflects exact teacher-student agreement, not neglected valuable knowledge. More broadly, predictive entropy measures uncertainty, not necessarily information or learning value; it can also identify ambiguity, noise, or teacher error. The asserted analogous relationship between feature magnitude and entropy is unsupported.

The weights are not shown to be mean-normalized. Since wEA lies in [0, log C], EA-KD changes the overall magnitude of the distillation loss—and hence its balance with the supervised objective—in addition to changing sample priorities. There is no constant-rescaling control, normalized-weight experiment, or fair retuning of baseline KD coefficients. The special reduction of the MLD+LS coefficient from 9 to 4 makes this confound particularly salient.

The student-entropy term has a weak rationale: entropy does not measure teacher-student disagreement, and equal entropies generally do not imply aligned distributions. The method can downweight a confident-teacher example even when the student is confidently wrong, while emphasizing examples where both distributions are highly uncertain. It is also unspecified whether gradients pass through the student-dependent weight. This materially changes the objective and reproducibility.

Evidence for the novel combined weight over teacher-only weighting is limited. In Table 9, its improvements over wbase are small and it is worse for FCFD (77.44 versus 77.50), contradicting the broad claim that the combination is superior. Comparisons with the closely related WTTM likewise show only very small gains.

Statistical comparisons are incomplete. Appendix C reports uncertainty only for EA variants because baseline papers provide means, so many gains of 0.1-0.4 points cannot be assessed under paired implementations or seeds. This also sits uneasily with the statement that all results were averaged over five runs.

Important implementation details are absent, including normalization and composition with the supervised loss, how per-image entropy weights detection proposals or spatial losses, and how token entropies are aggregated into sequence-level LLM weights. The task-dependent switch from T'=3 to T'=2 is not supported by corresponding ablations.

The t-SNE, CH-index, and loss-landscape analyses are under-specified and do not establish the claimed causal mechanism or improved generalization. Observing uncertain examples near decision boundaries is expected, while comparing arbitrary contour areas across different parameter spaces is difficult to interpret. Overall, the broad empirical signal is promising, but the scale confound, limited evidence for the student-adaptive component, and incomplete controlled statistics leave a slight preference for rejection.
